title: The Allegory of Lebanon
english: The Savior makes those who return from the evil they lived in to become followers of repentance regarding the sin they cast away. Just as it is not necessary to share the holy knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven with such people, so it is not fitting to compare the divine pearls—which are the words of the wise, decorating the inner man and his ears—to swine.

Does not the one disciplining them not feel insulted by the one saying, 'Compare with wise words your ear' (Prov 23:26), and by the one saying to the Word of God, 'Incline your ear to the words of my mouth' (Ps 89:8)? One must not compare the most beautiful and fine pearls, which the merchant of the kingdom seeks and hunts, to the interpreted swine, so that they do not trample them, having ignored their use and their beauty.

Having set forth testimonies to show that men have been treated as senseless, fake animals, it remains to set forth the Scriptures, showing how some men are praiseworthy in being similar in disposition and movement to certain animals. Are not these the very ones about whom the Savior says, 'My sheep hear my voice' (John 10:27), and again, 'I am the good shepherd and I lay down my life for the sheep' (John 10:11)?

The sheep of Christ are those establishing stability and gentleness, from whom the flock is completed, concerning which the Holy Spirit says through the prophet, 'And the Lord shall stand and see and shall shepherd his flock in strength' (Ezek 34:23). By such an analogy of 'the vessel of election' (2 Tim 3:15), Paul, speaking in Christ, took up the law 'you shall not muzzle an ox while it treads' (Deut 25:4), after setting it forth and bringing it in: 'Does God not care for the oxen? Or does he speak in any way about us?' (1 Cor 9:9), as the apostles make clear: 'that the plowman ought to partake of the plowing, and the one muzzling in hope of sharing' (1 Cor 9:10).

Finding many such things by the one paying attention to the reading of the God-breathed Scripture, lest the word be stretched beyond what is necessary, let him proceed regarding the Frankincense and its woods, having it thus: 'Open, O Frankincense, your doors, and let fire devour your cedars; let the pine wail, because the cedar has fallen, because the great princes have greatly suffered' (Zach 11:1-2).
You have been uprooted, oaks of Bashan, because the adjacent forest has been scattered.

The name Lebanon, for the sake of allegory, signifies either idolatry or pride and arrogance. For in the Song of Songs, the Church from the Gentiles is the bride of Christ; he says, 'Come from Lebanon, O bride, to ascend and pass through from the beginning of faith' (Song of Songs 4:17). Having received the word of Christ from the beginning, she comes to the one calling her from practical wickedness into moral virtue, and from ignorance and unbelief into a divine knowledge and a faith surpassing all through perfection.

Just as the spoken word 'Lebanon' signifies the impious service of idols and demons, so it represents pride in the saying, 'Lebanon shall be changed like Mount Hermon,' which is to say, the haughty and self-willed person shall be brought to the knowledge of the circumcision being led into the heart by the spirit; for Hermon is interpreted as the knowledge of circumcision. He who possesses this knowledge corrects his blindness, having learned from Jesus to be humble in heart and spirit.

By this twofold Lebanon, the prophet, who is inspired by the Spirit—rather, the Lord through him—calls out to open its doors, so that the cedars within the doors of it may be devoured by fire; and these are the idle demons and the haughty men, being crushed by the voice of the Lord, according to how it is sung in the 18th and 20th Psalm in this manner: 'The voice of the Lord crushing cedars; the Lord shall crush the cedars of Lebanon' (Psalm 28:16).

Since these are wild plants and do not bear edible fruit, in Isaiah it is written concerning others thus: 'The day of the Lord of hosts upon every arrogant and proud and high and lofty thing,' and after a few words: 'and upon every high cedar of Lebanon and upon every balsam tree of Bashan' (Isaiah 13:11). These such wild woods are grown up for idolatry and pride, being crushed and consumed by fire along with those who assemble sophistically about them, according to what is said in the same Isaiah: 'And the Lebanon shall fall with the lofty ones' (Isaiah 2:12).
For idolatry falls along with the demons who assemble with it and with sophist men; likewise also the haughty ones.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Oak and the Doors of Lebanon
english: Men with arrogance will fall when God opposes the proud, according to what is said in the writing of the Divine Proverbs: 'God opposes the proud' (Proverbs 16:5).

Regarding those thus exalted, those who are making blindness right through God send up a prayer, saying: 'Stretch out your hands against their pride to an end,' and with other things in the same Psalm: 'The pride of those hating you continually shall ascend to you' (Psalm 18:5).

Concerning the Lebanon which is given a double meaning, the divine word stands to open its gates. For when pride and idolatry have been opened and spread out, the fire of punishment will consume the cedars—those men who were exalted and the demons who look down upon others, not being other than 'the rulers of this age,' human and, as the Scripture says, 'fleshly wisdoms' (2 Corinthians 10:5), teaching 'heights puffed up according to the knowledge of God' (2 Corinthians 10:5).

When the cedars are devoured by fire, the firs lament, falling because of the stronger ones called cedars. And perhaps the unspiritual evil powers are called cedars, with the firs being the names of the heterodox and wise of this world and age who work under them.

The enigmatically spoken thing is released by the following word: 'Greatly the magnates were afflicted.' These are the ones swelling at the beginning, not men alone, but also the unspiritual rulers of this age.

Concerning these arrogant leaders, and in Nahum the prophet—and this is the seventh among the Twelve Prophets—it is said to Nineveh: 'And upon your glorious things they shall cast a lot, and all your magnates shall be bound in fetters' (Nahum 2:9), so that they might not do the forbidden things with easy release and hands not hindered; for it is for good to be hindered by 'hands entwined with iniquities.'

Having been greatly afflicted, the Basanite trees, the intertwined grove is torn down; and a grove is a place of wild trees bearing no nourishing fruit. And this is torn down, as its thickened vegetation is consumed by fire.
Lamenting trees do not turn out to be soulless plants, but, being led up allegorically, the souls of men who...

And opposing powers. It is not to be ignored that oaks, at times, signify all kinds of wood, and at other times a specific kind of wood. For when we call all woods oaks, the one cutting them is called a wood-cutter, and those made from them are called oak-wood, from which the name for oak-planks is derived, and the fruits of trees are called acorns. Regarding the general name, there is a specific kind of wood that is an oak, just like cypress, fir, or boxwood.

The doors of Lebanon, which the divine word protects from being opened, are the same as those of death, concerning which the singer in the ninth Psalm says about God: 'He lifts me up from the gates of death' (Psalm 9:13). Regarding these, as being the presence of evil, it is proverbially said to the wise: 'Do not approach the doors of her house' (Proverbs 7:18), and also concerning all false glory and impiety: 'A foolish and impudent woman becomes a loud-mouthed vessel, who does not know shame; for she sat on a seat by the doors of her own house, openly calling to those passing by' (Proverbs 9:13).

He who has drawn near to these doors strikes the doors about which the Savior said: 'Knock and it shall be opened to you' (Matthew 7:7), concerning which Wisdom says in Proverbs: 'Blessed is the man who listens to me, and the man who keeps my ways, staying awake at my doors every day, guarding the weights of my entrances' (Proverbs 8:34).

He who stays awake at these doors every day does not approach the doors of the prostitute and foolish woman who pretends, nor the doors of Lebanon which ought to be opened, the perceived security being destroyed, so that those lying within may appear as to what formlessness they possess, being hated and abandoned, for no one who wishes to see them is sober.

That which has been said concerning various woods is not spoken about soulless things, and it can be seen from many scriptures, especially prophetic ones, the exposition of which has already partially occurred; but it is sufficient to remember the prophet Ezekiel, as if Pharaoh and Assyria were woods. These are evil powers, the one the tyrant of Egypt and the other of Assyria, having roots and shoots raised up from much water, which, in imitation, envied the trees of the paradise of the enjoyment of God.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Ruin of False Leaders
english: Having large branches, imitating both firs and pines.

For how could they desire and imitate such great tyrants, to the point where it is possible to perceive them as tangible woods, in whose side-branches and limbs all winged creatures dwell and wild beasts give birth? In order that the prophecy might be easily understood, we set aside a part of it, having it as follows: 'Behold, an Assyrian cypress in Lebanon, and beautiful in its side-branches, and thick in its cover, and high in its greatness; and its beginning became in the midst of the clouds; water nourished it, the abyss raised it up, its rivers led around the plants of it, and its systems sent forth into all the woods of the plain. Because of this, its greatness was raised above all the woods of the plain, and its branches were enlarged and its side-branches were raised up from much water. In the spreading out of it in its side-branches, all the winged creatures of the heaven sheltered, and under its branches all the beasts of the plain gave birth, and in its shadow every multitude of nations dwelt' (Ezekiel 31:3). And it became beautiful in its height because of the multitude of its branches, because its roots became into much water. And many cypresses in the paradise of God and pines are not like its side-branches, and firs did not become like its branches; no wood in the paradise of God was made like it in its beauty because of the multitude of its branches, and the woods of the paradise of the enjoyment of God envied it.

The same or similar things have been said regarding what was spoken about Assyria and about Pharaoh. It should not be ignored that most of our brothers refer Pharaoh and Assyria to the devil, allegorizing them according to various thoughts, sometimes Pharaoh and sometimes Assyria. Those bringing this interpretation, let them say: what are the woods of the paradise that envied the devil, not being soulless but being living, rational animals, clearly? And it is nothing wonderful that the names of woods are categorized among rational animals, when even the wisdom of God is sometimes called a true vine, and sometimes the Tree of Life. The voice of weeping shepherds, because... (Zechariah 11:3).
Their greatness has been brought to misery; it is the roar of lions, because the thicket of the Jordan has been ruined.

The leaders of the peoples, who are shepherds of them both priestly and teaching-wise, turn out to be like sheep, while there are those presiding kingly rather than tyrannically as lions. And since both types of rulers are called shepherds and lions, it is necessary for all the subjects to be brought as sheep and other cattle, having a tendency toward the shepherds who graze, and toward the lions for the cattle. It has been said indeed in Proverbs: 'A lion is stronger than cattle, who does not turn away nor falls upon every cattle' (Proverbs 28:17).

Having fallen into misery, those under the teachers—rather, false teachers—and those lying tyrannically over them, the shepherds lament, not being sparing of the flocks, but having been deprived of shameful gains and for the sake of seizing pleasures, so that they might not serve the Law-giving God and Him who has given them to rule, but rather their own bellies.

Concerning the heterodox, the divinely-inspired Apostle writes, correcting the peoples of the Church: 'Do not be carried away by strange and varied teachings; for it is good to be established by grace' (2 Timothy 3:6-7), and again: 'For such teachers serve their own bellies, not Christ, deceiving the hearts of the simple through exploitation and greed' (2 Timothy 3:6-7), appearing as pastures through simplicity.

These, having suddenly come into perplexity, lament the things they desire to be pleasant, their greatness having been brought to misery, which they thought they had deceitfully; likewise also those who rule tyrannically roar, the Jordan having been ruined where they spoke and were hidden, thinking they had cover and safety through ferocity.
With many woods already being cut down and having been torn apart, as it has been said nearby, the adjacent forest is being torn apart.

Much is to be found in the Scripture signifying those presiding with raw and wild temper, being called lions approaching in judgment. Immediately indeed in the prophet Jeremiah, lions are said to be the hot-tempered ruler of Babylon and the tyrant of Assyria; and thus the prophecy has: 'Israel is a wandering sheep, lions have driven him; the first the king of Assyria devoured him, and later his bones the king...'
